blocks.text: Two Meanings of Affordance: Gibson vs Norman
Have you ever felt embarrassed at the entrance of a department store or a restaurant because you did not know whether to push or pull a door and ended up rattling it?
If so, rest assured.
It is not because you are clumsy, nor is it because you are careless.
It is because the design of the door is bad. More precisely, the affordance of the door is wrong.
Affordance.
This word, used in the worlds of design and psychology, refers to an invisible force lurking in every place of our lives.
Today, I will talk about the meaning of this mysterious word and the two different philosophies hidden within it.
What is Affordance?
The word Affordance is a coined word made from the English verb afford, which means to give or provide.
For example, suppose there is a chair of a reasonable height in front of you.
You look at the chair and feel that you can sit on it without thinking too deeply.
This is because the object called a chair affords, or provides, you with the action of sitting.
Alternatively, a flat floor affords walking, and a mug with a handle affords grasping.
In other words, affordance is the possibility of action that the environment or objects provide to us humans and animals.
We live our lives while subconsciously receiving these messages emitted by the environment, without thinking about them one by one.
Objects Speak Louder than Words
Well-designed products allow you to understand how to use them without reading the manual.
This is because the shape itself speaks to you about how to use it as an affordance.
For instance, look at the handle of a pair of scissors.
If one hole is small and the other is large, you instantly know how to put your fingers in, even without verbal explanation.
Conversely, a representative example of bad design is the door mentioned at the beginning where you do not know whether to push or pull.
If the door has a flat metal plate, we subconsciously try to push it.
If it has a handle, we subconsciously grab it and try to pull.
However, what if there is a door that has a handle but will not open unless you push it?
Our brains get confused, and we take the wrong action.
In technical terms, this is called a False Affordance.
Two Schools: Gibson and Norman
Now, this is the main topic of today.
Regarding the affordance I have explained so far, did you know that there are actually two largely different interpretations among experts?
One is the school of the psychologist James J. Gibson, the creator of this word.
The other is the school of the cognitive scientist Don Norman, who popularized this word in the design world.
Actually, although these two use the same word, their perspectives are surprisingly contrasting.
Norman's Affordance: Guidance as Design
When we say affordance in business or UI design fields, 90 percent of the time it is used in the meaning of Don Norman.
In 1988, he made this word widely known to the world in his masterpiece, The Design of Everyday Things.
For him, affordance is a message indicating how the object should be treated.
If a website link is blue and underlined, it is a message saying please click.
If there is a cracked wall in a game, it is a message saying you can break it with a bomb.
The true identity of Norman's affordance is a Perceived Hint for the designer to encourage the user to take action.
The protagonist here is the Designer's Intent.
There is a correct answer that they want the user to perform, and affordance is discussed as a technique to guide them there without hesitation.
Shocking Fact: It Was a Signifier
However, here I must tell you a fact that will make designers all over the world fall off their chairs.
Norman, the very person who popularized this word, made an outrageous correction in his book later in 2013.
He said the following.
"That thing everyone calls affordance should have really been called a signifier, or a symbol."
Surprisingly, Norman himself admitted that it was not affordance.
True affordance is a possibility that exists there even if it is hidden and invisible.
However, what Norman emphasized in the design world was a mark that informs the user of an action, like the shadow of a button or the handle of a door.
He argued that he should have renamed it a signifier, not affordance.
But a word once spread does not stop.
Even now, the habit of calling this signifier an affordance remains deeply rooted in the field.
Gibson's Affordance: Possibility in the Environment
On the other hand, the world of the creator James J. Gibson is more philosophical and vast.
For him, affordance is the value or possibility itself that the environment provides to animals.
Whether humans notice it or the designer's intent does not matter there.
For example, suppose there is a rock of a reasonable height in the forest.
No one designed that rock as something to sit on.
However, if that rock has the height and hardness to be sat on, that rock objectively affords, or provides, the act of sitting.
Even if you do not notice it, the possibility actually exists there.
The true identity of Gibsonian affordance is an objective relationship that exists between animals and the environment.
The protagonist here is Environment and Exploration.
There is no correct answer.
Users or animals explore the environment and discover their own way of using it.
That is Gibson's world.
Which Should Creators Look At?
How should we, game developers and designers, use these two properly?
The answer is that both are necessary, but mixing them is dangerous.
User interfaces such as menu screens and tutorials should be made from Norman's perspective, or signifiers.
Do not let the user get lost.
Buttons that can be pressed should look like they can be pressed, and you should place guidance thoroughly and clearly.
On the other hand, the core of gameplay and highly free experiences should be made from Gibson's perspective.
The fun of games like The Legend of Zelda: Breath of the Wild or Minecraft resides here.
Can I slide if I get on my shield on this slope?
Will this electric enemy get electrocuted if I throw it into water?
Instead of the developer putting out an arrow and guiding you to slide, they bury only the possibility in the environment called physics and wait for the player's discovery.
This is exactly the true identity of emergent play that gives players the supreme joy of thinking of it themselves.
Conclusion: Having Two Pairs of Glasses
When you use the word affordance, please stop for a moment.
Are you talking about the technique to convey clearly to the user, which is Norman's signifier?
Or are you talking about the depth of possibility that the user can discover, which is Gibson's affordance?
If you can use these two pairs of glasses properly, the world you create will be kind, yet possess bottomless depth.
